subject: biology

items.q: What is the relative advantage of sexual reproduction over asexual reproduction?
items.correct: Its offspring carry new gene combinations, giving the variation needed for a changed environment.
items.misconception: Its offspring gain the particular features that a changed environment comes to require.
items.why: Everyday language ('adapting to the environment') and the phrase 'variation needed for adaptation' suggest a purposeful response, so students slide into a Lamarckian view in which need generates the useful variation. Meiosis and fertilization generate new allele combinations blindly. The advantage of sexual reproduction is that among many varied offspring some are likely, by chance, to be adapted to a changed environment; natural selection then favours them. The variation is not directed by the change.
items.specStatementText: Asexual copies the parent; sexual mixes new combinations
items.random_wrong: Its offspring are better adapted than the parent in every environment, so more of them survive.

items.q: Aphids reproduce asexually through the summer, when conditions are stable and food is plentiful, and switch to sexual reproduction in autumn before conditions change. Which statement best explains this pattern?
items.correct: Summer clones copy an adapted genotype quickly; autumn sexual reproduction produces varied offspring for the changed conditions ahead.
items.misconception: Sexual reproduction is used in autumn because varied offspring are invariably fitter; the summer clones are a poor substitute produced under time pressure.
items.why: At GCSE and MYP variation is taught as the raw material of natural selection and therefore as a benefit, and asexual reproduction is presented as the primitive option, so students never weigh the cost of breaking up a successful genotype. Each mode has a relative advantage. Asexual reproduction copies a genotype that is already adapted to the existing environment into every offspring. Sexual reproduction produces new combinations of alleles and so the variation needed for adaptation to a changed environment, at the cost of a slower process, the need for a mate and the break-up of the parent's own combination.
items.specStatementText: Asexual copies the parent; sexual mixes new combinations
items.random_wrong: Sexual reproduction is used in autumn so that the offspring gain the specific cold-tolerance features that the coming winter demands.

items.q: In the sexual life cycle, what are the respective roles of meiosis and fusion of gametes in producing genetic variation?
items.correct: Meiosis breaks up parental allele combinations, and fusion of gametes produces new combinations.
items.misconception: Meiosis produces new alleles by mutation, and fusion of gametes combines the alleles of the two parents.
items.why: Students learn that meiosis 'creates genetic variation' and that mutation 'creates new alleles', and merge the two sources; the word 'new' is used for both. New alleles arise only by mutation. Meiosis shuffles existing alleles into new combinations: it separates the two alleles of each gene into different gametes and combines the alleles of different genes independently. Fusion of gametes then combines the shuffled sets of two parents.
items.specStatementText: Meiosis breaks up combinations; fertilization makes new ones
items.random_wrong: Meiosis is the only source of variation, and fusion of gametes merely restores the diploid number.

items.q: Two full siblings have the same two parents yet differ in many of their alleles. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Each gamete carried a different selection of parental alleles, and different gametes fused.
items.misconception: Each parent passed on the same half of its alleles both times, but the halves combined differently in each child.
items.why: The GCSE statement that 'offspring receive half their genes from each parent' suggests each parent hands over a fixed half, like cutting a document in two. Meiosis breaks up parental combinations of alleles. A heterozygous parent (Aa Bb) makes gametes AB, Ab, aB and ab in equal numbers; no gamete reproduces the parent's own combination, which is why full siblings differ from each other.
items.specStatementText: Meiosis breaks up combinations; fertilization makes new ones
items.random_wrong: New alleles arose by mutation during the meiosis that produced the gametes for each sibling.

items.q: In a fish species the female lays a few hundred large eggs in a nest and the male releases many millions of tiny sperm over them. Which statement explains the difference in size and number?
items.correct: Sperm must travel to the eggs, so they are small with few food reserves and can be produced cheaply in vast numbers.
items.misconception: Eggs are larger because each one carries far more of the genetic material than a sperm does.
items.why: Students equate cell size with the amount of DNA, and know that mitochondria (with their DNA) are inherited from the mother, so they assume the egg's bulk is genetic. Sperm and egg each contribute one haploid set of chromosomes; the nuclear DNA contribution is equal. The size difference is cytoplasm: the egg's food reserves. The prime difference between the sexes is that the male gamete travels to the female gamete, so it is small with less food reserves than the egg.
items.specStatementText: Why sperm are small and many, eggs large and few
items.random_wrong: The numbers should be equal since one sperm fertilizes one egg; the surplus sperm are defective ones.

items.q: A student annotates a diagram of the male reproductive system. Which annotation is correct?
items.correct: Epididymis: stores sperm while they mature after their production in the testis.
items.misconception: Urethra: carries urine only, because semen leaves through a separate duct in the penis.
items.why: The urethra is first met in the excretory system, and diagrams of the reproductive system often crop the bladder, so the shared route is not obvious. The sperm duct joins the urethra below the bladder. The urethra is the single tube through the penis that carries either urine or semen; a sphincter closes the bladder during ejaculation so the two do not pass at the same time.
items.specStatementText: The human reproductive systems, part by part
items.random_wrong: Seminal vesicle: stores the sperm until they are required for ejaculation.

items.q: A student annotates a diagram of the female reproductive system. Which annotation is correct?
items.correct: Oviduct: the site of fertilization; it moves the egg towards the uterus.
items.misconception: Uterus: the site of fertilization and, later, of implantation of the embryo.
items.why: The uterus is the organ associated with pregnancy in everyday knowledge, and simplified diagrams show sperm swimming 'up to the egg' inside the uterus. The egg released at ovulation is collected by the funnel of the oviduct, and sperm swim through the uterus into the oviduct to meet it. Fertilization occurs in the oviduct; the resulting embryo divides as it moves to the uterus over several days and only then implants in the endometrium.
items.specStatementText: The human reproductive systems, part by part
items.random_wrong: Endometrium: the thick muscular wall of the uterus that contracts during childbirth.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the feedback control operating in the days just before ovulation?
items.correct: High oestradiol stimulates LH secretion by positive feedback on the pituitary.
items.misconception: High oestradiol inhibits LH secretion by negative feedback, as in the rest of the cycle.
items.why: Negative feedback is the only kind of feedback students have used before (blood glucose, temperature), and oestradiol is introduced as the hormone that 'inhibits FSH', so its positive-feedback role is missed. The guide requires both positive and negative feedback. Rising oestradiol from the maturing follicle stimulates the pituitary to release more LH and FSH, which stimulates still more oestradiol: positive feedback that drives the LH surge and ovulation. After ovulation, progesterone with oestradiol inhibits FSH and LH by negative feedback.
items.specStatementText: The menstrual cycle and its hormones
items.random_wrong: Progesterone secreted by the pituitary stimulates oestradiol release by positive feedback.

items.q: Blood samples were taken from a woman on day 7 and day 21 of a regular 28-day cycle. Progesterone was very low on day 7 and high on day 21. What can be concluded about day 21?
items.correct: A corpus luteum has formed after ovulation and is secreting progesterone that maintains the endometrium.
items.misconception: The pituitary gland has increased its progesterone output in preparation for menstruation.
items.why: The pituitary is introduced as the 'master gland' that controls the cycle, and four hormones are learned as a group, so students place them all in the same gland. FSH and LH are pituitary hormones that act on the ovary. Oestradiol is secreted by the developing follicles and progesterone by the corpus luteum, the structure the follicle becomes after ovulation. The ovarian hormones then feed back on the pituitary.
items.specStatementText: The menstrual cycle and its hormones
items.random_wrong: Ovulation is about to occur, because the egg is released when menstruation begins on day 28.

items.q: What is the role of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) in the ovarian cycle?
items.correct: It stimulates the follicles to develop and to secrete oestradiol.
items.misconception: It causes the mature follicle to burst and release its egg at ovulation.
items.why: 'Follicle-stimulating' sounds as if it should do everything to the follicle, including making it burst, and FSH is the first hormone of the cycle in most narratives. FSH stimulates follicles to develop and secrete oestradiol. It is the LH surge around day 14 that causes ovulation and converts the emptied follicle into the corpus luteum. Both hormones rise together at mid-cycle, but ovulation is attributed to LH.
items.specStatementText: The menstrual cycle and its hormones
items.random_wrong: It is made in the corpus luteum to maintain the endometrium.

items.q: Which event occurs during fertilization in humans?
items.correct: The sperm nucleus enters the egg but the sperm's tail and mitochondria are destroyed.
items.misconception: The whole sperm enters the egg, so the embryo inherits its mitochondria from both parents.
items.why: GCSE diagrams show the sperm 'entering' the egg as a complete cell, and students know sperm are packed with mitochondria, so they assume these are passed on. The sperm's cell membrane fuses with the egg's cell membrane and the sperm nucleus passes into the egg cytoplasm; the tail and mitochondria are left behind or destroyed. Mitochondria, and mitochondrial DNA, are therefore inherited from the mother only.
items.specStatementText: What happens at fertilization in humans
items.random_wrong: The sperm and egg nuclei fuse into a single diploid nucleus before any cell division occurs.

items.q: A mutation in mitochondrial DNA is passed from a mother to all her children but is never passed on by a father. Which feature of fertilization explains this?
items.correct: The sperm's mitochondria are destroyed after its nucleus has entered the egg cytoplasm.
items.misconception: Sperm mitochondria enter the egg but are so outnumbered by the egg's own that their DNA is diluted away.
items.why: GCSE diagrams show the sperm 'entering' the egg as a complete cell, and students know sperm are packed with mitochondria, so they assume these are passed on. The sperm's cell membrane fuses with the egg's cell membrane and the sperm nucleus passes into the egg cytoplasm; the tail and mitochondria are left behind or destroyed. Mitochondria, and mitochondrial DNA, are therefore inherited from the mother only.
items.specStatementText: What happens at fertilization in humans
items.random_wrong: Each parent hands over exactly half of its DNA, and the mitochondrial DNA happens to fall in the mother's half.

items.q: IVF treatment begins with a drug that suspends the woman's own secretion of FSH and LH, followed by daily injections of FSH. Why is this done?
items.correct: Suspending her own cycle stops it interfering, so injected FSH can induce superovulation and many eggs be collected.
items.misconception: The injected FSH strengthens her natural cycle so that one egg is released at a predictable time.
items.why: Students know the normal cycle releases one egg and assume IVF works within it; the word 'stimulation' suggests strengthening the existing cycle. The normal secretion of hormones is suspended with a drug so that the woman's own cycle does not interfere, then artificial doses of hormones induce superovulation: the development and release of many eggs at once. Eggs are collected before ovulation rather than released naturally.
items.specStatementText: Hormones in IVF
items.random_wrong: The injections make fertilization possible in the oviduct once sperm are introduced into the body.

items.q: Where are the gametes of a flowering plant produced?
items.correct: Male gametes are produced inside pollen grains and female gametes inside ovules.
items.misconception: The pollen grains themselves are the male gametes and the ovules are the female gametes.
items.why: Pollination is taught as 'transfer of the male sex cells', and pollen is the visible thing that travels, so it takes the role of the sperm in the student's analogy. Gametes are produced inside pollen grains (male) and inside ovules (female). After pollination the pollen grain germinates on the stigma and its pollen tube carries the male gametes down the style; fertilization occurs when a male gamete fuses with the female gamete in the ovule.
items.specStatementText: Sexual reproduction in flowering plants
items.random_wrong: Male gametes are produced in the stigma and female gametes in the anther.

items.q: Garden pea flowers pollinate and fertilize themselves before they open. Which statement about reproduction in the pea is correct?
items.correct: It is sexual, because meiosis makes the gametes and they fuse at fertilization.
items.misconception: It is asexual, because only one parent plant takes part in the process.
items.why: Students define asexual reproduction as 'one parent' rather than 'no meiosis and no fusion of gametes', so anything a single plant does on its own is classed as asexual. The guide states that reproduction in flowering plants is sexual even if a plant species is hermaphroditic. The test is whether meiosis and fusion of gametes occur, not the number of parents. Self-fertilization is sexual reproduction with reduced variation; a runner or bulb is asexual reproduction.
items.specStatementText: Sexual reproduction in flowering plants
items.random_wrong: Fertilization is complete as soon as the pollen has landed on the flower's stigma.

items.q: Which structure of an insect-pollinated flower is correctly paired with its function?
items.correct: Stigma: sticky surface on which pollen grains land and then germinate.
items.misconception: Stigma: produces pollen grains and sheds them onto the bodies of visiting insects.
items.why: Both are small structures on stalks at the centre of the flower, both begin with vowel-heavy unfamiliar names, and on a labelled diagram their labels sit side by side. Stamen = anther (makes and releases pollen) on a filament. Carpel = stigma (sticky surface that receives pollen), style (through which the pollen tube grows) and ovary (contains the ovules). In an insect-pollinated flower both are positioned so that a feeding insect brushes them.
items.specStatementText: Parts of an insect-pollinated flower
items.random_wrong: Ovary: holds the seeds until the fruit ripens and the seeds are dispersed.

items.q: In one flower species the anthers shed their pollen and wither several days before the stigma of the same flower becomes receptive. How does this promote cross-pollination?
items.correct: The flower's own pollen is gone when its stigma is receptive, so only pollen brought from another plant can pollinate it.
items.misconception: It does not; a flower that has both stamens and carpels will pollinate itself whatever the timing of the two.
items.why: Students reason from proximity: the anthers are millimetres from the stigma, so self-pollination seems unavoidable unless the parts are on separate flowers. Different maturation times for pollen and stigma within one flower are a method of promoting cross-pollination in hermaphroditic flowers: the flower's own pollen is not available when its stigma is receptive, so pollen brought by insects or wind from another plant is what lands.
items.specStatementText: How plants avoid pollinating themselves
items.random_wrong: It ensures the pollen reaches other flowers on the same plant, which is precisely what cross-pollination means.

items.q: Which of these is a method that promotes cross-pollination?
items.correct: Male and female flowers borne on separate individual plants.
items.misconception: Transfer of pollen between different flowers on the same plant.
items.why: Self-pollination is pictured as pollen falling onto the stigma of its own flower, so any movement between two flowers looks like 'crossing'. Pollen moving between flowers on the same plant is still self-pollination, because the gametes come from one genotype. Cross-pollination requires two plants and is what separate male and female plants, different maturation times, and animal or wind transfer are promoting.
items.specStatementText: How plants avoid pollinating themselves
items.random_wrong: Seeds carried away from the parent plant by animals.

items.q: In a self-incompatible plant species, pollen from a flower lands on the stigma of the same flower and germinates, but no seed is set. Which statement about self-incompatibility explains this?
items.correct: It stops a plant's own pollen from fertilizing its eggs, so preventing inbreeding.
items.misconception: It works by physically preventing the flower's own pollen from ever landing on its stigma.
items.why: The methods of promoting cross-pollination just learned (separate flowers, different timing) are all about preventing pollen arriving, so students expect self-incompatibility to work the same way. Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism, not a physical one. The plant's own pollen may land and even germinate, but the matching alleles are recognized and the pollen tube is stopped. This ensures that male and female gametes fusing during fertilization are from different plants.
items.specStatementText: Self-incompatibility keeps gametes from different plants
items.random_wrong: It prevents inbreeding, which would otherwise cause harmful new mutations in the offspring.

items.q: What is the difference between pollination and seed dispersal?
items.correct: Pollination moves pollen to a stigma before fertilization; dispersal moves seeds after it.
items.misconception: They are the same process: the wind or insect that carries the pollen also carries the seeds away.
items.why: Both processes involve something being carried away from a flower by wind or animals, and the same agents (wind, animals) appear in both lists. Pollination happens first and involves pollen and a stigma; fertilization follows, ovules become seeds and the ovary becomes a fruit; only then does dispersal happen, carrying seeds or fruits away so seedlings do not compete with the parent. The guide requires the two to be distinguished.
items.specStatementText: Seeds are dispersed, then germinate on stored food
items.random_wrong: Pollination is the fertilization of the flower; dispersal is the release of the fertilized pollen grains.

items.q: A barley grain germinating in dark, moist soil grows a root and a shoot for several days. Where do the energy and materials for this growth come from?
items.correct: Starch stored in the grain is hydrolysed by amylase to soluble sugars, which are moved to the embryo and respired.
items.misconception: The emerging shoot photosynthesizes using the small amount of light that reaches it through the soil.
items.why: Students associate plant growth with photosynthesis alone and forget that a seed underground has no light and no leaves. The embryo grows using the food reserves stored in the seed. Amylase produced in response to gibberellin hydrolyses starch to maltose, which is converted to glucose for respiration and for making new cell walls. Only when the shoot emerges and leaves open does photosynthesis take over.
items.specStatementText: Seeds are dispersed, then germinate on stored food
items.random_wrong: The grain absorbs dissolved food from the surrounding soil along with the water that it takes up.

items.q: A child whose hypothalamus cannot release GnRH fails to enter puberty, although the pituitary gland and gonads are normal. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Without GnRH the pituitary does not increase LH and FSH release, so the gonads are not stimulated to raise sex hormone production.
items.misconception: GnRH normally acts directly on the gonads, so without it they cannot make sex hormones; the pituitary gland plays no part in puberty.
items.why: 'Gonadotropin-releasing hormone' contains the word gonad, so students assume the hormone targets the gonads, skipping the pituitary step. GnRH is released by the hypothalamus and travels the short distance to the pituitary, where it stimulates release of the gonadotropins LH and FSH. It is these that act on the gonads. The chain is hypothalamus, pituitary, gonad, sex hormones, changes of puberty.
items.specStatementText: Puberty starts in the hypothalamus
items.random_wrong: The gonads should start puberty on their own, so the fault must in fact lie in the testes or the ovaries themselves.

items.q: Which comparison of spermatogenesis and oogenesis in humans is correct?
items.correct: Each meiosis yields four sperm but only one egg, because oogenesis divides the cytoplasm unequally.
items.misconception: Each meiosis yields four gametes in both processes, but three of every four eggs degenerate before birth.
items.why: Meiosis is taught as 'one cell produces four haploid cells', and spermatogenesis fits that pattern exactly, so students apply it to oogenesis too. In spermatogenesis the cytoplasm divides equally, giving four small sperm. In oogenesis the cytoplasm divides unequally at each division so that one cell, the egg, receives almost all of it as food reserves; the other products are polar bodies. Gametogenesis therefore results in different numbers of sperm and eggs and different amounts of cytoplasm.
items.specStatementText: Making sperm and making eggs
items.random_wrong: Both processes continue to produce new gametes from puberty right through to old age.

items.q: A man produces about 100 million sperm per day. A woman is born with about a million egg-forming cells arrested in meiosis, and releases only about 400 eggs in her lifetime. Which conclusion do these figures best support?
items.correct: Egg-forming cells are all made before birth and are then used sparingly over a lifetime.
items.misconception: Eggs are produced continuously like sperm, but nearly all are broken down before they can be ovulated.
items.why: Spermatogenesis is continuous from puberty, and students generalize gametogenesis from the male case; the monthly release of an egg also looks like monthly production. Oogenesis begins in the foetus: mitosis, cell growth and the start of meiosis all happen before birth, and no new egg-forming cells are made afterwards. Spermatogenesis produces millions of sperm daily from puberty onwards. This difference in timing underlies the difference in numbers.
items.specStatementText: Making sperm and making eggs
items.random_wrong: Each of the million cells produced four eggs, most of which were not released from the ovary.

items.q: In an experiment, eggs treated so that they could not carry out the cortical reaction were each entered by several sperm. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Without the cortical reaction the zona pellucida is not hardened, so further sperm can still digest through it and fuse.
items.misconception: The cortical reaction is what lets the first sperm in, so blocking it should have stopped fertilization altogether.
items.why: Two reactions with unfamiliar names are learned together and neither name says which cell it belongs to; 'cortical' does not obviously mean the egg's cortex. Acrosome belongs to the sperm: the acrosome is the vesicle in the sperm head whose enzymes digest the zona pellucida. Cortical belongs to the egg: cortical granules just beneath the egg membrane are released when the first sperm fuses, changing the zona so that polyspermy is prevented.
items.specStatementText: One sperm in, all others out
items.random_wrong: Sperm bore through the egg membrane with their enzymes, so hardening the zona could not have stopped them.

items.q: Which statement about the blastocyst and implantation is correct?
items.correct: The blastocyst is a hollow ball with an inner cell mass and implants in the endometrium about a week after fertilization.
items.misconception: The zygote itself implants in the endometrium immediately after fertilization, before it has divided into a ball of cells.
items.why: Students learn 'fertilization then implantation' as consecutive steps and, believing fertilization happens in the uterus, see no reason for a delay. Fertilization occurs in the oviduct. The zygote divides repeatedly by mitosis as it is moved towards the uterus, developing into a blastocyst by about day 5 to 7, and only the blastocyst can implant in the endometrium.
items.specStatementText: From zygote to blastocyst to implantation
items.random_wrong: The blastocyst is a solid ball of identical cells, every one of which goes on to form part of the foetus.

items.q: A home pregnancy test strip contains monoclonal antibodies. Which statement explains how the test indicates pregnancy?
items.correct: The antibodies bind hCG in the urine, and only an implanted embryo or its placenta produces hCG.
items.misconception: The antibodies bind progesterone, which is present in the urine at a high level only during a pregnancy.
items.why: Progesterone is the hormone most associated with pregnancy in the student's mind, and its level is indeed high in pregnancy. Progesterone is also high in the luteal phase of every cycle, so it cannot distinguish pregnancy. hCG is secreted only by an implanted embryo or its placenta and appears in the urine within days, so the test uses monoclonal antibodies specific to hCG.
items.specStatementText: Pregnancy tests detect hCG with monoclonal antibodies
items.random_wrong: The antibodies bind hCG released into the blood by the mother's pituitary gland when she becomes pregnant.

items.q: A foetus in the uterus has fluid-filled, collapsed lungs, yet its blood is oxygenated. How does oxygen reach the blood of the foetus?
items.correct: It diffuses from maternal blood into foetal capillaries in the placental villi.
items.misconception: Maternal blood carrying oxygen flows through the placenta into the blood vessels of the foetus.
items.why: Phrases such as 'the baby gets oxygen from the mother's blood' and diagrams that colour the placenta uniformly red suggest a direct connection. The two circulations stay separate. Oxygen, glucose and other nutrients diffuse or are transported from maternal blood into foetal blood across the villi; carbon dioxide and urea pass the other way. Separation protects the foetus from the mother's higher blood pressure and from immune attack on mismatched blood groups.
items.specStatementText: The placenta supplies the foetus without mixing bloods
items.random_wrong: The placenta filters oxygen out of the mother's blood while blocking all harmful substances.

items.q: Which sequence correctly describes the hormonal changes that bring about childbirth?
items.correct: Progesterone falls, contractions begin, and oxytocin rises by positive feedback as the cervix is stretched.
items.misconception: Progesterone rises to a peak that triggers contractions, and oxytocin then falls until the baby is born.
items.why: Students expect a major event to be caused by a hormone increasing, and progesterone is 'the pregnancy hormone', so they assume its peak causes birth. Progesterone maintains pregnancy by keeping the uterine muscle relaxed. The changes of childbirth are triggered by a fall in progesterone, allowing oxytocin secretion to increase. Contractions stretch the cervix, stimulating more oxytocin release: positive feedback that continues until the baby is born.
items.specStatementText: Progesterone keeps pregnancy going; its fall lets birth begin
items.random_wrong: Oxytocin is kept at a steady level by negative feedback so that the contractions stay regular.

items.q: Early epidemiological studies found that women taking HRT had a lower incidence of coronary heart disease (CHD). Later randomized controlled trials found that HRT slightly increased CHD risk. Which conclusion is best supported?
items.correct: The correlation was not causal: women on HRT tended to have higher socioeconomic status, which itself lowers CHD risk.
items.misconception: The early studies were correct because they involved far more women than the trials did, so their result should be preferred.
items.why: Students judge studies by sample size and date rather than by design, and have not met the idea of a confounding variable. An observational study, however large, cannot remove differences between women who choose HRT and those who do not. Randomization is what removes them. The HRT case is the standard NOS example of a correlation that was mistaken for a cause-and-effect relationship until a controlled experiment was done.
items.specStatementText: HRT and heart disease: correlation is not cause
items.random_wrong: HRT must lower CHD risk in most women, and the trials must have happened to sample an unusual group of women.

items.q: In a mammal, removing the ovaries (and with them the corpus luteum) early in pregnancy ended the pregnancy, but the same operation late in pregnancy did not. What does this show?
items.correct: Progesterone is secreted by the corpus luteum at first and later by the placenta once it has formed.
items.misconception: The placenta maintained the pregnancy in both cases; the early loss was caused by the stress of surgery.
items.why: The placenta is learned as the organ of pregnancy, and students assume it is present and functioning as soon as pregnancy begins. Initially the placenta has not developed. Continuity of pregnancy is maintained by progesterone secreted first by the corpus luteum (which hCG prevents from degenerating) and then, once it has formed, by the placenta. If the corpus luteum fails in the early weeks, progesterone falls and the pregnancy is lost.
items.specStatementText: Progesterone keeps pregnancy going; its fall lets birth begin
items.random_wrong: Later in pregnancy the mother's pituitary gland takes over progesterone secretion, so the ovaries are no longer needed.

items.q: Which organisms reproduce asexually?
items.correct: Many organisms in every kingdom, including many plants (by runners, bulbs and tubers), fungi, cnidarians such as Hydra, and some animals such as aphids, as well as bacteria; many species use both modes.
items.misconception: Asexual reproduction is something only bacteria and other simple microorganisms do.
items.why: Binary fission in bacteria is the only asexual reproduction most students meet before IB, so they file 'asexual' with 'prokaryote'. Asexual reproduction is widespread among eukaryotes, especially plants, and many species switch between asexual reproduction when conditions are stable and sexual reproduction when they change (aphids and Daphnia are standard examples). The choice of mode is about the environment, not about how simple the organism is.
items.specStatementText: Asexual copies the parent; sexual mixes new combinations
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does fertilization itself add to genetic variation, or only restore the diploid number?
items.correct: It does both: because any one of the male gametes may fuse with any one of the female gametes, fertilization produces combinations of alleles that neither parent possessed.
items.misconception: All the variation among offspring comes from meiosis; fertilization simply joins two gametes and restores the diploid number.
items.why: Textbooks list the 'sources of variation in meiosis' as crossing over and independent assortment, and treat fertilization as the mechanical end of the cycle, so students credit only meiosis. Meiosis breaks up parental allele combinations; fusion of gametes produces new ones. Which sperm fuses with which egg is random, so fertilization is itself a source of the new gene combinations that sexual reproduction is valued for.
items.specStatementText: Meiosis breaks up combinations; fertilization makes new ones
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do males and females produce similar numbers of gametes?
items.correct: No. Because male gametes are small and cheap they are produced in enormous numbers (hundreds of millions per ejaculation in humans), whereas the large, costly female gametes are produced in far smaller numbers (one per cycle in humans).
items.misconception: Since one sperm fertilizes one egg, males and females must produce roughly the same number of gametes.
items.why: Diagrams of fertilization show a single sperm meeting a single egg, and students reason from the one-to-one outcome back to one-to-one production. From the prime difference (the male gamete travels, so it is small with few food reserves) follow the differences in number: many cheap sperm are made because only a tiny fraction complete the journey, while each egg represents a large investment and so few are produced. These differences underlie the different reproductive strategies of males and females.
items.specStatementText: Why sperm are small and many, eggs large and few
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is the sperm small: because so many are made, or because it has to travel?
items.correct: Because it has to travel to the egg. Being small and carrying little food makes it motile and cheap to produce, and being cheap is what allows so many to be made.
items.misconception: Sperm are small because they are produced in such large numbers that there is only a little material for each one.
items.why: Students learn 'sperm are small and numerous' as a pair of facts and reverse the direction of cause: the number seems the striking fact, so smallness is explained by it. The IB chain of reasoning runs the other way. The prime difference is that the male gamete travels to the female gamete; from this follows its small size and lack of food reserves, and from that follow the large numbers produced and the different reproductive strategies of the sexes.
items.specStatementText: Why sperm are small and many, eggs large and few
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where are sperm stored between production and ejaculation?
items.correct: In the epididymis, the coiled tube on the surface of each testis, where they also mature.
items.misconception: Sperm are stored in the seminal vesicles until ejaculation.
items.why: The name 'seminal vesicle' sounds like a vessel for semen or sperm, and its position along the sperm duct near the prostate suggests a holding chamber. The seminal vesicles and prostate gland are accessory glands: they add alkaline, fructose-containing fluid to sperm to form semen during ejaculation. Sperm are produced in the testes and stored in the epididymis, then carried along the sperm duct.

items.q: What is the endometrium?
items.correct: The inner lining of the uterus, rich in blood vessels, which thickens each cycle for implantation and is shed at menstruation.
items.misconception: The endometrium is the thick muscular wall of the uterus that contracts during childbirth.
items.why: Students learn the uterus as 'a muscular organ' and the endometrium as 'the uterus lining that thickens', and conflate thickening of the lining with the thick muscle wall. The uterus has a muscular wall (the myometrium, whose name is not required) and an inner lining, the endometrium. It is the endometrium that thickens under oestradiol and progesterone, receives the implanting blastocyst, and breaks down during menstruation. The muscle wall is not shed.
items.specStatementText: The human reproductive systems, part by part
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What triggers menstruation?
items.correct: The fall in progesterone (and oestradiol) when the corpus luteum degenerates about ten days after ovulation, which removes the support for the thickened endometrium.
items.misconception: Menstruation is brought on by a rise in hormone levels at the end of the cycle.
items.why: Students expect an event to be caused by a hormone 'switching on', and graphs are read by looking for peaks rather than for the drop that precedes day 1. Progesterone from the corpus luteum maintains the endometrium. If no embryo implants there is no hCG, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone and oestradiol fall, the endometrium breaks down and menstruation begins. The low hormone levels also release the pituitary from negative feedback, so FSH rises and the next cycle starts.
items.specStatementText: The menstrual cycle and its hormones
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do the sperm and egg nuclei fuse into a single diploid nucleus?
items.correct: No. The two nuclear membranes dissolve and all the condensed chromosomes from both nuclei take part in a joint mitosis, which directly produces two diploid nuclei in the first two cells of the embryo.
items.misconception: The sperm nucleus fuses with the egg nucleus to form one diploid zygote nucleus, which then divides by mitosis.
items.why: GCSE teaches 'the nuclei fuse to form a zygote', and the word fertilization is defined as fusion of nuclei, so students picture a single merged nucleus as the end of fertilization. In humans the haploid nuclei do not merge before division. Their nuclear membranes break down, the chromosomes of both sets attach to a shared spindle, and the first mitotic division of the zygote produces two diploid nuclei. The first cells with a single diploid nucleus each are therefore the two cells produced by this first division.
items.specStatementText: What happens at fertilization in humans
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does the sperm nucleus get inside the egg?
items.correct: The cell membrane of the sperm fuses with the cell membrane of the egg, so the sperm nucleus passes into the egg cytoplasm through the joined membranes.
items.misconception: The sperm uses its enzymes to bore a hole through the egg's cell membrane and pushes its way in.
items.why: Students hear that the acrosome enzymes 'digest a way in' and assume this applies to the cell membrane as well as to the outer coat of the egg. Enzymes are needed only to penetrate the zona pellucida, the coat outside the egg membrane. Entry itself is by membrane fusion: the two cell membranes join, the sperm nucleus enters, and the tail and mitochondria are destroyed. A hole in the egg membrane would be lethal to the egg.
items.specStatementText: What happens at fertilization in humans
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where does fertilization happen in IVF?
items.correct: Outside the body, in a dish in the laboratory; the fertilized embryos are then transferred into the uterus.
items.misconception: In IVF the hormones and sperm are given to the woman so that fertilization happens inside her body as normal.
items.why: IVF is confused with artificial insemination, and 'fertility treatment' in everyday use covers both; the Latin phrase in vitro is not understood. In vitro means in glass. Collected eggs are mixed with sperm in the laboratory, and one or more resulting embryos are placed in the uterus to implant. The hormone treatment is for superovulation, not for fertilization.
items.specStatementText: Hormones in IVF
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is pollination the same as fertilization?
items.correct: No. Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma; fertilization is the later fusion of a male gamete with the female gamete inside the ovule, after the pollen tube has grown down the style.
items.misconception: Pollination is plant fertilization: when the pollen lands on the stigma the flower has been fertilized.
items.why: In animals the arrival of the sperm at the egg and fertilization are almost the same event, and 'pollinate' is used loosely in everyday speech to mean 'fertilize'. Pollination, pollen development (germination and pollen tube growth) and fertilization are three separate steps. Pollination can occur without fertilization following, for example if the pollen is incompatible and its tube fails to grow.
items.specStatementText: Sexual reproduction in flowering plants
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is inside the ovary of a flower?
items.correct: Ovules, each containing a female gamete; an ovule becomes a seed only after its gamete has been fertilized.
items.misconception: The ovary of a flower contains the seeds, waiting to be released when the fruit ripens.
items.why: The words ovule and seed are met together and the ovary is known as the part that 'becomes the fruit containing the seeds', so students backdate the seeds to the flower. Before fertilization the ovary contains ovules. A pollen tube carries a male gamete to each ovule and after fertilization the ovule develops into a seed (with the embryo inside) and the ovary into the fruit. An unpollinated flower sets no seed.
items.specStatementText: Parts of an insect-pollinated flower
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does inbreeding reduce vigour?
items.correct: Because breeding between related individuals increases homozygosity, so harmful recessive alleles already in the population are more often inherited in the homozygous state and expressed; genetic diversity also falls.
items.misconception: Inbreeding is harmful because it causes new mutations in the offspring.
items.why: Students know that inbred offspring often show genetic defects and reach for mutation as the only mechanism they know for producing defects. Inbreeding does not create alleles; it changes their combinations. Self-pollination is the extreme case and leads to decreased genetic diversity and vigour. Self-incompatibility mechanisms ensure that the gametes fusing at fertilization are from different plants, keeping the population outbred.
items.specStatementText: Self-incompatibility keeps gametes from different plants
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a seed absorb food from the soil to germinate?
items.correct: No. It absorbs water (and oxygen) from the soil, but the organic food for growth comes from the seed's own reserves until the seedling can photosynthesize.
items.misconception: Seeds germinate by drawing nutrients and food from the soil, which is why seeds need good soil.
items.why: Gardening advice about 'rich soil' and the everyday idea that plants 'feed' from the soil lead students to treat soil as the seedling's food source. Germination needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Water activates the embryo and allows the mobilization of food reserves; the growth and development of the embryo are fuelled by respiration of the seed's own stores. Mineral ions from soil are needed later, but they are not food.
items.specStatementText: Seeds are dispersed, then germinate on stored food
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What starts puberty?
items.correct: An increase in the release of GnRH by the hypothalamus, which triggers increased LH and FSH secretion by the pituitary; these stimulate the gonads to increase sex hormone production, and the sex hormones cause the changes of puberty.
items.misconception: Puberty begins when the testes or ovaries spontaneously start to make sex hormones on their own.
items.why: The visible changes of puberty are explained at GCSE by 'testosterone' and 'oestrogen', so students place the origin of puberty in the gonads that make them. The gonads respond to signals: increased GnRH from the hypothalamus in late childhood is the trigger, GnRH raises LH and FSH release from the pituitary, and LH and FSH stimulate the testes or ovaries to secrete more steroid sex hormones. The gonads do not act independently.
items.specStatementText: Puberty starts in the hypothalamus
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Has the egg completed meiosis when it is released at ovulation?
items.correct: No. The cell released at ovulation has completed only the first division of meiosis; the second division is completed only if a sperm enters it.
items.misconception: The egg finishes both divisions of meiosis in the ovary and is a fully mature haploid gamete when it is ovulated.
items.why: Diagrams label the released cell 'egg' and gametes are defined as haploid cells, so students assume meiosis is complete at release. Oogenesis pauses twice: early in the first division before birth, and after the first division is completed just before ovulation. The second meiotic division, producing the second polar body, is triggered by entry of the sperm. The two divisions of meiosis in oogenesis are therefore spread over many years.
items.specStatementText: Making sperm and making eggs
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the structure of a blastocyst?
items.correct: A hollow ball of cells with a fluid-filled cavity, an inner cell mass that will form the foetus and an outer layer of cells that attaches to the endometrium and later forms part of the placenta.
items.misconception: A blastocyst is a solid ball of identical cells, all of which go on to form the baby.
items.why: The early embryo is pictured as 'a ball of cells' and students assume all the cells are equivalent because they came from one zygote. By the blastocyst stage the cells have already begun to differ: the outer layer will contribute to the placenta and only the inner cell mass gives rise to the foetus. The cavity makes the blastocyst hollow.
items.specStatementText: From zygote to blastocyst to implantation
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which tissue produces hCG?
items.correct: The embryo itself, from its outer cells after implantation, and later the developing placenta.
items.misconception: hCG is a hormone released by the mother's ovary or pituitary gland when she becomes pregnant.
items.why: Every other hormone of the cycle comes from the pituitary or the ovary, so students assign the new hormone to one of the glands they already know. hCG is produced by the embryo or the developing placenta, not by the mother's glands. That is precisely why detecting it in urine indicates pregnancy: it is present only when an embryo has implanted. It maintains the corpus luteum so progesterone secretion continues.
items.specStatementText: Pregnancy tests detect hCG with monoclonal antibodies
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the placenta keep out all harmful substances?
items.correct: No. It exchanges substances by diffusion and transport according to their properties, so small lipid-soluble molecules such as alcohol and nicotine, some drugs and some viruses cross it.
items.misconception: The placenta acts as a filter that blocks everything harmful, letting through only what the foetus needs.
items.why: The placenta is described as a 'barrier' and as 'protecting the foetus', which students read as an intelligent filter. The placenta's exchange processes are physical: diffusion down concentration gradients, facilitated diffusion and active transport across the large surface area of the villi. Nothing selects for 'harmful'. This is why alcohol, smoking and some infections during pregnancy damage the foetus.
items.specStatementText: The placenta supplies the foetus without mixing bloods
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Did the early studies show that HRT protects against coronary heart disease?
items.correct: No. They showed a correlation between taking HRT and lower CHD incidence; randomized controlled trials later showed HRT slightly increases CHD risk, and the correlation was explained by HRT users having higher socioeconomic status, which itself lowers CHD risk.
items.misconception: A strong correlation found in a large study of many women is enough to show that HRT causes the lower rate of heart disease.
items.why: Large sample sizes feel convincing, and 'HRT users had less heart disease' is naturally read as 'HRT gave them less heart disease'. Correlation is not cause and effect. In an observational study the women who chose HRT differed from those who did not, in socioeconomic status among other things, and that difference has a causal relationship with lower CHD risk. Only a randomized controlled trial, which allocates treatment at random, can separate the effect of HRT from the effect of who takes it.
items.specStatementText: HRT and heart disease: correlation is not cause
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do the testes produce semen?
items.correct: No. The testes produce sperm; semen is sperm plus the fluids added by the seminal vesicles and prostate gland during ejaculation.
items.misconception: Semen is made in the testes, and the glands along the sperm duct only store it.
items.why: Semen is the visible ejaculate and the testes are the only 'factory' students know, so the whole product is credited to them; the words sperm and semen are also used interchangeably in everyday speech. Sperm are produced in the testes and stored in the epididymis. During ejaculation they pass along the sperm duct, where the seminal vesicles add fluid containing fructose and the prostate gland adds alkaline fluid; the mixture that leaves through the urethra is semen.
items.specStatementText: The human reproductive systems, part by part
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the growth of a germinating seedling just the seed swelling with water?
items.correct: No. Water uptake starts germination, but the increase in the embryo's tissues comes from new cells and cell walls built from the seed's food reserves, using energy from cell respiration.
items.misconception: A germinating seed grows by taking in water and swelling; no food or respiration is needed until it has leaves.
items.why: The first visible change is the seed swelling, and mass measurements of seedlings grown in water are dominated by water, so growth is equated with water uptake. Germination involves the growth and development of the embryo, which requires the mobilization of food reserves: stored starch is hydrolysed to sugars that are respired for ATP and used to build new cells. A germinating seed's dry mass falls as reserves are used, even while its wet mass rises.
items.specStatementText: Seeds are dispersed, then germinate on stored food
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does only one sperm normally fertilize an egg?
items.correct: Because as soon as the first sperm fuses with the egg membrane the cortical reaction alters the zona pellucida so that no further sperm can pass through; many sperm reach the egg but only one enters.
items.misconception: Polyspermy does not happen because only one sperm ever manages to reach the egg.
items.why: Fertilization is often described as a race won by a single sperm, so students imagine one arrival rather than many sperm around the egg. Dozens of sperm typically reach and attach to the zona pellucida. Polyspermy is prevented actively: the acrosome reaction lets one sperm penetrate the zona pellucida, and the cortical reaction triggered by its entry prevents other sperm from passing through.
items.specStatementText: One sperm in, all others out
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where do the antibodies in a pregnancy test come from?
items.correct: They are monoclonal antibodies manufactured in the laboratory, built into the test strip, that bind specifically to hCG.
items.misconception: A pregnancy test works because the pregnant woman's immune system makes antibodies against hCG, which appear in her urine.
items.why: Students have learned that antibodies are produced by the body in response to an antigen, so they assume any antibody involved must be the woman's own. hCG is the woman's own hormone (made by her embryo or placenta) and her immune system does not respond to it. The test strip contains monoclonal antibodies, produced from a single clone of cells, that bind hCG in the urine and produce a visible line.
items.specStatementText: Pregnancy tests detect hCG with monoclonal antibodies
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does the foetus obtain oxygen?
items.correct: Oxygen diffuses from the mother's blood into the foetal blood in the capillaries of the placental villi and is carried from the placenta to the foetus; the foetal lungs are not used.
items.misconception: The foetus breathes with its lungs inside the uterus, taking oxygen from the amniotic fluid.
items.why: Breathing is the only way students know of obtaining oxygen, and the foetus is seen surrounded by fluid, so they imagine it breathing that fluid. The foetal lungs are collapsed and fluid-filled until birth. All gas exchange happens in the placenta: oxygen diffuses from maternal blood into foetal blood across the large surface area of the villi, and carbon dioxide diffuses the other way. This is one of the exchange processes that allows the foetus to be retained in the uterus.
items.specStatementText: The placenta supplies the foetus without mixing bloods
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If the correlation between HRT and lower CHD was not cause and effect, was the correlation itself wrong?
items.correct: No. The correlation was genuine: women on HRT really did have lower CHD incidence. What was wrong was the inference of cause; the correlation arose because HRT users tended to have higher socioeconomic status, which lowers CHD risk.
items.misconception: When a correlation turns out not to be cause and effect, the correlation must have been a chance or mistaken result.
items.why: Students treat 'not causal' as meaning 'not real', because they have no model of a third variable producing a true correlation between two things that do not affect each other. A correlation can be real and still not causal when a confounding variable (here socioeconomic status) influences both the exposure and the outcome. The randomized controlled trials did not show the early data were wrong; they showed that the causal interpretation of them was wrong.
items.specStatementText: HRT and heart disease: correlation is not cause
